feedback: If a child groups by colour, size or 'the pretty ones', restrict the collection to a single colour and size so appearance cannot be the criterion, forcing attention to a property.

When a placement breaks the chosen rule (e.g. a cone, which has a curved surface, dropped into 'no curved surface'), point to the mismatch and ask which property decides membership — the property, not the look.
Prompt consistency: 'Does every shape in this group follow your rule?' If membership drifts for a borderline shape, revisit the stated rule.

Watching a shape such as a triangular prism move to the other hoop when the rule changes — it has no curved surface but does have triangular faces, so it belongs in a different group under each rule — is the moment 'a sort needs one property' becomes concrete. (A cube would stay put, since it has neither a curved surface nor a triangular face.)
activities.intendedInsight: A sort rests on one geometric property held constant and applied to every item; the same collection can be grouped validly in more than one way depending on which property you choose.
learnerActions: Take a physical, mixed tray of handleable 2-D shapes, 3-D solids and everyday objects.

Choose ONE geometric property as the rule (e.g. 'has a curved surface / has no curved surface') and place every item into one of two sorting hoops or a labelled two-set frame. Check that the rule makes sense for every item in the tray: a flat 2-D shape such as a circle has a curved side (edge) but no curved surface, so either agree how 2-D shapes are judged or pick a rule that fits both 2-D and 3-D items (e.g. 'has a curved edge or surface / has none').
Say the rule aloud ('all of these have a curved surface') and check: does EVERY shape in this group follow my rule?
Now scatter the SAME shapes and re-sort them by a different property (e.g. 'has a triangular face / has no triangular face'); notice which shapes move to a different hoop and why.
activities.title: Sort a real tray two ways on an 'is / is not' rule

feedback: If a child cannot state a single rule that every group member satisfies, model one aloud ('these all have a triangular face') and check each member against it.

If the inferred rule is a non-geometric feature such as colour or size, point to two members of the SAME group that differ in that named feature (e.g. two different colours) yet were grouped together, so the child sees appearance cannot be the rule and looks for the shared geometric property.
Confirm success when the child's continuation placements all satisfy the same stated property.
activities.intendedInsight: Making the hidden criterion explicit forces attention onto defining properties and shows that a good sort rests on one rule every member satisfies.
learnerActions: Look at a set someone else has already sorted into two groups, with the rule hidden.
Infer and state the geometric property that was used to make the two groups.
Continue the sort by placing a few more shapes into the correct group, keeping the rule constant.
Then set your own 'guess my rule' challenge for a partner.
activities.title: Guess my rule

feedback: If recounts give different totals, ask how to be sure each side/face is counted once and model marking each one as it is counted — scaffold the counting, do not reteach the whole topic.
If a shape lands in the wrong group, check whether its faces/vertices were miscounted rather than whether the rule was wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: A count-based sort is only as reliable as the count; marking each feature once prevents losing track and keeps the sort consistent.
learnerActions: Hold a real solid and mark each face, edge or vertex with a wipe-clean pen as you count it, so you count each one exactly once.
Record the count, then use it as the sorting rule (e.g. 'sort solids by number of faces' or 'six or more vertices / fewer than six vertices').
Recount a solid a second way and check you get the same total; if not, find where you lost track.
Place each solid in the correct group based on the verified count.
activities.title: Count faces, edges and vertices accurately before sorting
